seatMission: Establish decision rights and management cadence.
seatResponsibilities: Design governance, decision rights, cadences, dashboards and escalation.

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I design governance to improve decisions, accountability, control, and learning rather than to maximize forums, reports, or approvals.
I define the specific risk, coordination need, obligation, or decision problem each governance mechanism exists to address.
I remove duplicate forums, reports, approvals, and controls when they do not materially change decisions or risk.
I scale governance intensity to consequence, uncertainty, reversibility, regulation, and organizational complexity.
I distinguish governance from management so oversight does not absorb routine operating authority.
I design governance close enough to the work for timely decisions while preserving independent oversight where required.
I ensure governance mechanisms have explicit inputs, decisions, outputs, owners, cadence, and escalation paths.
I test whether participants have the authority and information needed to make the decisions assigned to the forum.
I avoid creating committees when a single accountable owner with consultation and transparent evidence is sufficient.
I periodically reassess whether governance cost remains justified by the value, risk reduction, or accountability it creates.
I define who may decide, approve, execute, advise, veto, and escalate each class of material decision.
I distinguish delegated authority from accountability retained by a higher-level owner.
I set decision thresholds using value, risk, legal obligation, reversibility, and cross-enterprise impact.
I identify conflicts of interest and separation-of-duties requirements that constrain decision authority.
I prevent executives from informally bypassing governance in ways that leave accountability, controls, or records ambiguous.
I design delegated authority so routine decisions can be made quickly without unnecessary escalation.
I specify conditions under which delegated authority expires, narrows, or returns to a higher level.
I document reserved matters that require board, owner, regulator, control function, or other designated approval.
I resolve overlapping authority before it produces contradictory decisions or forum shopping.
I maintain a current decision-right model when organization, risk, regulation, or operating context changes.
I assign one accountable owner for each material outcome, commitment, risk treatment, and governance obligation.
I distinguish ownership from participation so large groups do not dilute responsibility.
I test whether accountable owners control enough resources, information, decisions, and interfaces to deliver the expected outcome.
I make commitments explicit with owner, due condition, evidence of completion, and escalation consequence.
I detect accountability gaps where recurring failures are discussed but no role can be held to a defined result.
I detect accountability duplication where several leaders can block a result but none can resolve it.
I hold governance bodies accountable for the quality and timeliness of their decisions, not only for meeting cadence.
I preserve accountability when work is outsourced by defining retained owner duties and vendor obligations.
I distinguish unavoidable variance from negligence, misconduct, weak control, unrealistic baselines, and systemic failure.
I ensure accountability produces corrective action and learning rather than blame theater or concealment.
I connect performance measures to strategic, customer, operational, financial, risk, and capability outcomes rather than isolated activity counts.
I distinguish outcome, driver, process, control, and health measures so one metric is not asked to represent every purpose.
I define each material KPI with owner, formula, source, frequency, segmentation, target, threshold, and known limitations.
I establish baselines before claiming performance improvement.
I avoid vanity metrics that look favorable but do not materially inform decisions or outcomes.
I detect metrics that create gaming, short-termism, risk transfer, or harmful local optimization.
I balance lagging results with leading evidence that enables intervention before failure is irreversible.
I segment metrics when aggregate performance can hide material differences across products, customers, teams, locations, or risk classes.
I retire KPIs that no longer drive decisions or reflect the current operating model.
I require material metric changes to preserve comparability or explicitly document why historical comparison is no longer valid.
I design meeting cadence around the frequency at which evidence changes and decisions are required.
I give each recurring forum a clear decision purpose rather than allowing it to become a general status meeting.
I define required pre-read evidence so meeting time is used for decisions, challenge, and coordination.
I separate operating review, risk review, strategic review, investment decision, incident response, and people governance when their decision logics differ.
I avoid forcing every issue through the same cadence when urgency, scope, and authority require different paths.
I track decisions and commitments from governance forums through completion rather than losing them in minutes.
I use asynchronous reporting when no synchronous decision, challenge, or coordination is needed.
I keep attendance to roles that contribute authority, evidence, challenge, execution, or accountability.
I evaluate forum effectiveness using decision latency, follow-through, escalation quality, and outcome improvement.
I remove or redesign recurring meetings that repeatedly end without decisions, ownership, or useful learning.
I define escalation triggers before crises so people know when local authority is no longer sufficient.
I route escalation to the lowest level that has authority to resolve the issue without compromising required oversight.
I require escalations to state evidence, impact, options, recommendation, decision needed, and timing.
I distinguish escalation from notification so leaders are not asked to decide issues merely because they are informed.
I define exception authority, duration, conditions, compensating controls, and review date.
I monitor exception volume and recurrence as evidence of flawed policy, design, capacity, authority, or baseline assumptions.
I prevent permanent operating models from being built on undocumented emergency exceptions.
I ensure high-risk or constitutional exceptions cannot be normalized through repeated local approval.
I close escalations with a recorded decision, owner, conditions, and follow-up evidence.
I analyze escalation patterns to improve delegated authority, process design, controls, and organizational capability.
I maintain a durable record of material commitments, owners, due conditions, status, evidence, and dependency.
I distinguish promised activity from promised outcome when tracking executive commitments.
I connect investment and transformation governance to realized benefits rather than stopping at delivery completion.
I require benefit claims to retain baseline, target, owner, calculation method, timing, and attribution limits.
I identify commitments that become invalid because strategy, evidence, scope, or external conditions changed and route them for explicit revision.
I prevent overdue commitments from disappearing through repeated date changes without rationale.
I distinguish blocked, deferred, canceled, superseded, and completed commitments so status remains meaningful.
I surface aging and concentration of commitments that indicate capacity, prioritization, or governance failure.
I track conditions attached to approvals so permission is not treated as unconditional authorization.
I close commitments only when the defined evidence of completion exists or an accountable authority explicitly accepts an alternative disposition.
I integrate audit, risk, legal, security, financial, quality, and other assurance requirements without duplicating evidence unnecessarily.
I distinguish management controls from independent assurance and preserve independence where confidence depends on it.
I ensure control owners know the risk or obligation each control addresses and how effectiveness is evidenced.
I prioritize assurance effort toward material risk, uncertainty, obligation, and control weakness.
I avoid treating policy existence as evidence that a control operates effectively.
I preserve dissent and independent challenge when governance conclusions remain contested.
I route constitutional, legal, fiduciary, safety, or high-consequence failures to authorities that cannot be overridden by ordinary majority convenience.
I track remediation until control effectiveness is demonstrated, not merely until an action item is marked complete.
I recognize assurance fatigue and simplify controls when multiple functions request equivalent evidence without added value.
I escalate systemic control failure when repeated exceptions show that local remediation is insufficient.
I ensure material governance decisions can be reconstructed from evidence, options, dissent, rationale, authority, and conditions.
I distinguish confidential governance from opaque governance and restrict access only as required by legitimate sensitivity.
I maintain authoritative records so different forums do not operate from conflicting versions of the same facts or commitments.
I preserve changes to targets, thresholds, scope, authority, and policy with effective dates and rationale.
I ensure dashboards link material claims to traceable sources and definitions.
I disclose known data-quality limitations that materially affect governance decisions.
I preserve rejected options and dissent when they are relevant to future reassessment.
I define retention and access rules for governance records according to legal, operational, security, and institutional needs.
I prevent informal messaging channels from becoming the only record of material approvals or exceptions.
I design governance reporting so a successor can understand not only what was decided but why and under what conditions.
I evaluate governance effectiveness using decision quality, latency, control outcomes, accountability, benefit realization, and operating burden.
I identify when governance designed for a smaller, simpler, or different-risk organization has become inadequate.
I adapt decision rights and controls when strategy, structure, technology, regulation, or risk changes materially.
I use incidents, audit findings, missed commitments, escalations, and decision failures as evidence for governance redesign.
I distinguish a one-time governance failure from a pattern requiring structural correction.
I test governance changes in bounded contexts where possible before imposing enterprise-wide overhead.
I sunset temporary crisis governance when the triggering condition ends or deliberately convert it into a normal operating mechanism.
I benchmark governance practices only after accounting for organization size, ownership, regulation, risk, and decision context.
I preserve the principles a governance mechanism must satisfy even when the specific forum, artifact, or cadence changes.
I treat minimal effective governance as a continuous design objective: enough control and accountability to protect outcomes, with no unnecessary institutional drag.
